column3: It closely parallels those who do not expect the meeting demanding a different revelation on their own terms.
The declaration of divine oneness does not materially clarify the demand or the arrogance in the focus.
Its destructive force called transgressive offers only a remote lexical parallel to the people's great transgression.
Arrogant elites issue a coercive religious demand, illuminating the focus's self-exalting posture.
It directly reverses the demanded sight of angels: their arrival brings no good news to the criminals.
Seeing alleged partners exposes their false claims, a related judgment-scene correction of a false appeal to the Lord.
It gives the same demand for an angel and states that granting it would bring the matter to final judgment.
The contrasting condition of the Garden's people adds no specific insight into the focus's demand.
It explains how arrogance can leave signs visible yet still produce refusal, relevant to the demand to see.
Its judgment dialogue shows the arrogant and the weak blaming each other after their rejection is exposed.
The descent of the Book and testimony is broad evidentiary context but not a close parallel to the demand.
What deniers had pressed for becomes an unwelcome seen reality, clarifying the reversal implicit in the focus.
The arrogant leaders and their followers confront regret and punishment after seeing its reality.
The later local scene of remorse develops the consequence of the surah's rejecting and arrogant stance.
It names disbelief in meeting the Lord as the underlying issue behind an objection framed as a question.
It repeats the focus's defining description of those who do not expect meeting God and locates their heedlessness.
The local criticism of those who neither hear nor reason helps characterize the focus's unreasonable demand.
The destruction of Aad does not add a close link to the demand for angels or sight of the Lord.
Angels descend to reassure the steadfast, forming a meaningful contrast with the criminals' demanded angelic sight.
Its settled punishment is only general background for the consequence of the focus's rebellion.
Self-purification lightly contrasts with the focus's self-magnification but does not address its demand.
At the final exposure, followers appeal to the arrogant for relief and find no escape from punishment.
The local description of being gathered to Hell gives broad outcome context without explaining the objection.
Its persistence in transgression and aversion directly parallels the focus's description of great overstepping.
The anticipated arrival of angels or the Lord shows that such a demand belongs to an irreversible reckoning.
The nearby warning of Hell's perception and sound supplies punitive context for the ensuing encounter scene.
Its call to compete in a worthy good does not clarify the arrogant demand in the focus.
It again identifies those without hope of meeting God and explains the delayed consequence of their rebellion.
The contrast between transient worldly life and the lasting Hereafter is only indirect context for their denial.
A great sign shown to Pharaoh is a distant parallel to the focus's insistence on a chosen visible proof.
The arrogant explicitly reject what believers affirm, illustrating arrogance as a response to revealed truth.
A later local demand that revelation descend in a preferred form closely echoes the focus's attempt to set its terms.
Hopeful certainty of meeting the Lord provides a limited contrast to the focus's lack of such expectation.
The question about absent people in Hell does not materially illuminate the focus's demand.
The marked punishment for excess is only broad consequence context.
Its affirmation that the heart did not deny what it saw concerns a distinct visionary setting.
False claims of revelation, arrogance, angels, and humiliating punishment converge in a related accountability scene.
The local descent of angels completes the focus's requested event in the surah's reversed judgment setting.
The prohibition on self-praise offers only a general ethical contrast to their self-exaltation.
Not expecting an accounting supplies a close conceptual counterpart to not expecting the meeting.
Turning away arrogantly from recited signs explains why additional demanded signs would not yield receptivity.
Individual responsibility and return to God are too general to clarify the particular objection.
Elites treat ordinary humanity and low social status as grounds to reject a messenger, similar to the focus's objection.
The local list of destroyed peoples supplies distant warning context only.
Its ambiguous reference to a meeting does not add a clear parallel to the focus.
Angels confront people who wronged themselves at death, a related but distinct angelic reckoning scene.
The angelic declaration to Abraham does not clarify the criminals' demand.
The record of every small and great matter has no specific connection to the focus.
Its punishment follows persistent overstepping of a prohibition, illustrating the consequence of transgression.
The immediately preceding local warning that oppressors taste great punishment frames the focus's condemning context.
The earth casting out its contents does not add a close link to the demand or arrogance.
A shown sign that increases people in great transgression cautions that visible proof need not cure rebellion.
The image of futile works does not specifically clarify the focus's claim.
Its hypocritical changes of speech across social settings are not a close parallel.
Calling only the true God offers a limited contrast to the focus's presumptuous demand concerning the Lord.
The local description of those avoiding falsehood does not explain the focus.
It tightly joins arrogant self-exaltation with the false assumption that people will not return to God.
It explicitly pairs the arrival of angels or the Lord with the point at which later faith cannot benefit.
The exception for the people of the right has no direct bearing on the focus.
Seeing the least evil deed is a general judgment principle rather than a parallel to the objection.
Angels meet self-wronging people who attempt submission and denial, a related final encounter.
The local command for great striving does not substantially clarify the unbelievers' demand.
Its concern about disclosing information to opponents is unrelated to the focus.
A faithful request for a descending sign contrasts with the focus's defiant demand but adds little after closer cases.
The angels' mission against criminals supplies only broad punishment context.
Unseen divine support contrasts with the focus's demand for visible angels but remains indirect.
Its request to defer fighting is not closely related to demanding angels or sight of God.
The local accusation that the Quran is fabricated shows rejection in the same surah but not the specific demand.
It identifies the most intense rebellion within groups for judgment, closely echoing the focus's great transgression.
The request for doubled punishment is general and does not explain their arrogant claim.
It names doubt about meeting the Lord, directly clarifying the focus's lack of expectation of that meeting.
Arrogance and wicked plotting ultimately recoil on their authors, supplying a consequence for the focus's attitude.
The grateful speech and call to Paradise form a distant contrast without clarifying the focus.
The local worship of powerless others gives broad disbelief context but not the requested encounter.
The unavoidable meeting with death and return offers only a general counterpart to meeting the Lord.
God's complete transcendence above what people say corrects the presumption embedded in their demand to see Him.
Signs in horizons and selves present an alternative evidentiary path to the truth they seek to dictate.
The Garden's moderated climate has no meaningful relation to the focus.
Belief only after seeing painful punishment shows why a demand for sight is not saving receptivity.
The local promise of lasting blessing does not directly explain the focus's arrogant demand.
After transgressing, people demand the promised consequence on their terms, closely paralleling the focus's posture.
The brothers' confession of fault does not add a close connection.
The immediately preceding verse explains the human-messenger setting that prompts the objection at 25:21.
Arrogance after clear proofs illustrates that the focus's demand is not simply a lack of available evidence.
It closely parallels the objection that an angel should come with the messenger rather than accepting revelation.
The local portrait of people responsive to their Lord's signs contrasts with the focus's refusal to respond properly.
The visible renewal of the earth is unrelated to the specific demand and arrogance.
Its vision of great dominion does not clarify the focus.
The local descent of purifying rain is not a close parallel to the demanded descent of angels.
Their arrogance when divine oneness is proclaimed exposes resistance to the Lord's exclusive authority.
The contrast of believers' reward and deniers' Hell is too general to add to the focus.
The invitation to inspect creation does not closely address their demand for angelic descent.
The promise of Paradise provides no specific interpretive addition.
Its praise of those who are not arrogant supplies a limited ethical contrast to the focus.
Seeing the impending reality as near is only a broad eschatological parallel.
A startled judgment that a man is an angel is only a remote parallel to demanding angels.
Pharaoh's coercive claim to superior authority lightly parallels the focus's self-exalting stance.
Revelation's imagined effect of humility contrasts sharply with the arrogant response in the focus.
Rejecting guidance after it is clear gives broad context but no specific connection to the demand.
Seeing an evil act as good explains the distorted perception that can sustain the focus's arrogant objection.
The same surah explicitly objects that no angel was sent down with the human messenger, directly setting up the focus's demand.
It directly challenges the messenger to bring angels if he is truthful, closely matching the focus's stipulated proof.
It explains that angels are sent down only with the truth and then no respite remains, answering the focus's request with finality.
The demand to see God openly before believing is a direct antecedent to the focus's demand to see the Lord.
A people demand to be shown God openly, and the verse identifies the demand as part of a grave rebellious history.
Even angels descending and every sign speaking would not make hardened rejecters believe, directly qualifying the focus's requested sign.
The demand to bring God and the angels visibly is an especially close parallel to both elements of the focus's objection.
Its escalating list of conditions for belief shows the same effort to make revelation answer human-imposed terms.
The elite reject a human messenger and ask why angels were not sent down to them, closely paralleling the focus's social objection.
The demand that angels accompany a messenger reflects the same insistence on externally chosen credentials.
Those without knowledge ask why God does not speak to them or send a sign, providing a broader parallel to demanded direct access.
The insistence that a sign must produce belief is countered by the warning that such a sign may still not bring faith.
Moses' request to see the Lord, answered by the overwhelming manifestation, is a boundary case that clarifies the gravity of visual demand.
The objection that God sent a human messenger rather than another kind of messenger closely matches the premise behind the focus's complaint.
It states the proper purpose of God sending angels, with revelation and warning rather than submission to a rejecter's demand.
The messenger's denial that he is an angel gives limited context for the mistaken standard applied to human messengers.
Noah's refusal to claim angelic status is a limited counterpoint to demands that a messenger meet an angelic expectation.
